standard.title: Compare target language and English structures using metalanguage
standard.description: compare some target language structures and features with those of English, using some familiar metalanguage
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recognise familiar target language features and compare with English using grammatical metalanguage (AC9LS4U03). They apply metalanguage to grammar comparison. They have not yet compared grammatical features in text production contexts, analysed persuasive language effects, or explored informal and youth language varieties.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students compare target language and English language structures and features using metalanguage — including text-type conventions, persuasive language, informal variety and vocabulary pattern connections.

nodes.label: Comparing grammatical structures and text conventions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare grammatical structures and text conventions across the target language and English using metalanguage — identifying what each language does differently and explaining it.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare at least three grammatical features across the target language and English using metalanguage; identify at least one text convention that differs.
nodes.typical_width: Use metalanguage in both languages; recognise grammatical elements associated with specific text types; compare traditional text conventions across the two languages; compare subject-predicate structure and word order; compile comparison graphic organisers.
wider: Create a bilingual grammar comparison chart covering at least five features — each with a target language example, an English example and an explanation of the difference
Analyse a target language and English text of the same type side by side — use metalanguage to annotate every grammatical difference
nodes.hinge_reason: Metalanguage precision for grammatical comparison is the analytical tool for all subsequent language analysis. Students who use metalanguage loosely cannot engage in the text evaluation and analysis work at subsequent bands.

response_modes.reason: Metalanguage precision develops through repeated application across multiple texts and comparison tasks before it becomes a reliable analytical tool.

success_criteria: Uses at least three metalanguage terms accurately in comparing target language and English grammatical features
Identifies at least one text convention that differs between the target language and English

nodes.label: Persuasive language, informal varieties and vocabulary patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and compare persuasive language in target language and English texts, and explore informal language varieties and vocabulary patterns.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two persuasive language features in a target language text and compare them with English equivalents; identify at least one example of informal language variety or vocabulary pattern.
nodes.typical_width: Compare advertisements and public signs for persuasive and directive language across both languages; explore informal language used by young people in target language communities; compare affective language features across the two languages; notice vocabulary patterns for extending word knowledge.
wider: Create a target language persuasive text using at least three persuasive techniques — annotate each with metalanguage
Research informal language used in target language communities — explain each term, find any English parallel and describe what each reveals about youth culture

response_modes.reason: Persuasive language and informal variety awareness develops through exposure to varied authentic target language texts — advertisements, signs, social media, informal speech.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Informal language and youth variety connects target language learning to genuine contemporary culture. Students who understand these forms can engage with authentic contemporary materials inaccessible to those with only formal register competence.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two persuasive language features in a target language text and names each using metalanguage
Identifies at least one informal language feature or vocabulary pattern and explains its social or communicative function
